concept.name: Dragonfly doji
concept.definition: A doji variant in which the open, high, and close are equal or nearly equal, leaving a long lower shadow and little or no upper shadow (a T shape). Technical analysts read it as intraperiod selling that was fully absorbed by buyers, and treat it as a possible bullish reversal sign when it appears after a decline; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor.
concept.intuition: Sellers drove price sharply lower during the period, but buyers pushed it all the way back to the opening level, showing demand underneath the market.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: open, high, and close cluster at or near the same price (small tolerance), while the low sits far below, so the lower shadow dominates the range. It is the single-candle mirror of the gravestone doji.
concept.failure_modes: Its reversal implication fails often in strong downtrends, where the bounce back to the open is only temporary short covering. In quiet markets it occurs frequently and carries no signal.
concept.misconceptions: A dragonfly doji is not automatically bullish; after an advance it can mark exhaustion instead. It requires confirmation from the following candle before it supports any directional hypothesis.
concept.example: In a downtrend, a stock opens at 40.00, falls to 37.50 intraday, then recovers to close at 40.00. The resulting dragonfly doji suggests sellers failed to hold the lows, and traders watch for a higher close the next day as confirmation.
